segments.t: KTPH001Hardening optionsKTPH002 are a set of production-quality techniques you can ask the AI to bake into a script it generates or rewrites. Instead of writing the same instruction ("add error handling", "make it re-runnable", "give it a KTPH000") by hand every time, you tick the techniques you want and KorTTY turns each one into a precise rule that is appended to the AI prompt. The result is a script that behaves like something a careful engineer would ship: it fails loudly instead of silently, cleans up after itself, logs what it does, and can be run again without surprises.
The same eleven options are used everywhere KorTTY generates or improves a script, so they behave identically no matter where you start from.
Not the same as Input hardening

Hardening options shape KTPH000how the script is writtenKTPH001 (structure, error handling, logging, CLI). The separate KTPH002Input hardeningKTPH003 panel instead asks the AI to build a concrete KTPH004input-validation guard blockKTPH005 into the script that checks parameters and input files at run time. The two appear side by side and can be combined.
The KTPH000Hardening optionsKTPH001 panel shows up in these places:
KTPH000Terminal → Generate Workflow ScriptKTPH001 (the KTPH002WorkflowKTPH003 button after an agent run)
Collapsible KTPH000Hardening optionsKTPH001 panel (collapsed by default)
No panel — the default all-on selection is applied automatically
KTPH000Snippet editor → AI Code → Improve robustnessKTPH001
Options panel with all boxes ticked
You confirm the dialog; KorTTY rewrites the complete snippet when any hardening rule is active
KTPH000Snippet editor → AI Code → Custom improvement…KTPH001
Options panel plus a free-text instruction field
You confirm the dialog; KorTTY rewrites the complete snippet when any hardening rule is active
KTPH000Snippet editor → AI Code → Full code analysisKTPH001
Collapsible KTPH000Hardening optionsKTPH001 panel at the bottom of the window, with a live KTPH002(N)KTPH003 count of ticked options in its title; korTTY remembers whether you left it open or closed

KTPH000Improve readabilityKTPH001 and KTPH002Improve performanceKTPH003 deliberately do KTPH004notKTPH005 show hardening options — those actions are meant to stay close to the original code. Hardening options appear only where adding robustness is the point: KTPH006Improve robustnessKTPH007, KTPH008Custom improvementKTPH009, KTPH010Full code analysisKTPH011, and the two workflow-script generators.
Every option is KTPH000ticked by defaultKTPH001. Untick the ones you do not want. An unticked option contributes nothing to the prompt.

In KTPH001Improve robustnessKTPH002 and KTPH003Custom improvementKTPH004, active hardening rules are applied to the KTPH005complete snippetKTPH006, even if you marked only one region. This is required because options such as strict mode, a configuration block, KTPH000, and a final summary must change the prologue or epilogue rather than only the selected lines. If you use KTPH007ClearKTPH008 and leave Input hardening off, the ordinary improvement remains limited to the selected region. The complete-snippet result is still shown in the before/after review and is rejected if the AI abbreviates unchanged code with an omission marker.
Below the options, three buttons help you manage the selection:
KTPH000ClearKTPH001 — untick every option (generate/apply with no hardening rules).

KTPH000SaveKTPH001 — remember the current selection permanently. From then on, every hardening panel opens with your saved selection instead of the all-on default — so you can set your preferred hardening once and have it applied everywhere.

Each ticked option becomes one authoritative hardening rule that KorTTY appends to the request sent to the AI (under KTPH004Apply these hardening techniques:KTPH005 in the snippet editor, or KTPH006ADDITIONAL REQUIREMENTS:KTPH007 in the workflow generator). In the Full code analysis apply flow, every selected rule is additionally assigned its own mandatory identifier: the AI returns the identifiers it completed in one compact list, and korTTY rejects the whole response if any identifier is missing. Explicit CLI and guard literals such as KTPH000, KTPH001, KTPH002, and KTPH003 must also be present when the corresponding options are selected. Workflow generation also adds the corresponding target-language idioms — for example the Bash spelling of strict mode — only while that option is selected. Unticking an option removes both its rule and its option-specific language idioms; KTPH008ClearKTPH009 therefore sends no hardening behaviour, apart from neutral requirements needed to produce valid code in the chosen language.
The wording of each rule KTPH000adapts to the target languageKTPH001:
KTPH000Imperative scriptsKTPH001 — Bash, Python, Perl, Ruby, PowerShell, Windows-CMD and AppleScript get the imperative phrasing (flags, traps, exit codes, …).

KTPH008Declarative artefactsKTPH009 — Ansible playbooks, and snippets whose language is KTPH000/KTPH001 or contains KTPH002, get Ansible-idiomatic phrasing instead (KTPH003/KTPH004/KTPH005, KTPH006, KTPH007, check mode, …).
So the KTPH003ideaKTPH004 of each option is the same everywhere, but a Bash script gets a KTPH000 style rule while an Ansible playbook gets an KTPH001 / KTPH002 style rule for the very same tick-box.
The eleven options fall into two groups by their effect on the script:

KTPH000Behaviour-preserving hardeningKTPH001 (the first seven) only add documentation, logging, structure, and safety nets. They make the script sturdier and easier to read KTPH002without changing what it actually doesKTPH003. These are safe to leave on for almost any script.

KTPH000Behavioural / interactive changesKTPH001 (the last four) can change control flow or add a command-line interface — precondition gates, re-run detection, a dry-run mode, argument parsing. Leave them off if you want the rewrite to stay as close as possible to the original behaviour.
Each option below lists what it is for and the exact rule KorTTY sends to the AI — for imperative scripts and for Ansible playbooks.
KTPH000What it is forKTPH001 — Stop the script the moment something goes wrong instead of blindly continuing on a half-failed state.
KTPH004Imperative scriptsKTPH005 — Enable the language's strict / abort-on-error mode (for example KTPH000 in Bash, KTPH001 with KTPH002 in PowerShell, KTPH003 in Perl).
KTPH002Ansible playbooksKTPH003 — Validate prerequisites with KTPH000/KTPH001 so bad state fails the play immediately.
KTPH000What it is forKTPH001 — Guarantee that a failure is reported clearly and that any temporary state (temp files, mounts, locks) is cleaned up even when the script aborts.
KTPH002Imperative scriptsKTPH003 — Add an error trap / KTPH000 / KTPH001 block that reports failures and cleans up temporary state.
KTPH003Ansible playbooksKTPH004 — Use KTPH000/KTPH001/KTPH002 so failures are caught and cleanup always runs.
KTPH000What it is forKTPH001 — Let whoever calls the script (a scheduler, a CI job, another script) tell KTPH002whyKTPH003 it failed, not just KTPH004thatKTPH005 it failed.
KTPH000Imperative scriptsKTPH001 — Use distinct, documented non-zero exit codes for distinct failure classes.
KTPH001Ansible playbooksKTPH002 — Make failing tasks stop the play with a clear message (KTPH000 where sensible).
KTPH000What it is forKTPH001 — Make the script's progress visible and debuggable without cluttering normal output.
KTPH002Imperative scriptsKTPH003 — Emit timestamped log messages to stderr and support a KTPH000/KTPH001 flag.
KTPH002Ansible playbooksKTPH003 — Use the KTPH000 module for progress output (visible with KTPH001).
KTPH000What it is forKTPH001 — Collect the values you are most likely to change (paths, hostnames, package names) in one obvious place instead of scattering them through the script.
KTPH000Imperative scriptsKTPH001 — Hoist all literals (paths, hosts, packages) into a clearly commented configuration block near the top.
KTPH001Ansible playbooksKTPH002 — Hoist all literals into a KTPH000 block at the top.
KTPH000What it is forKTPH001 — End with a short report so the operator can see at a glance what happened.
KTPH000Imperative scriptsKTPH001 — Print a final summary of what was done (with success/failure counts).
KTPH001Ansible playbooksKTPH002 — End with a KTPH000 summary of what changed.
KTPH000What it is forKTPH001 — Produce code that passes the language's standard linter, so it reads consistently and avoids common footguns.
KTPH000Imperative scriptsKTPH001 — Follow the language style guide and keep it linter-clean (for example ShellCheck-clean for Bash).
KTPH001Ansible playbooksKTPH002 — Follow KTPH000 conventions and use fully-qualified module names.
KTPH000What it is forKTPH001 — Fail fast, before touching anything, if the environment isn't ready — a missing command, insufficient privileges, or no network.
KTPH000Imperative scriptsKTPH001 — Before doing work, verify required commands, privileges (root/sudo) and connectivity.
KTPH002Ansible playbooksKTPH003 — Add KTPH000/KTPH001 checks for required privileges, packages and connectivity before any change.
KTPH000What it is forKTPH001 — Make the script safe to run a second time: steps that are already done are detected and skipped instead of repeated or erroring out.
KTPH000Imperative scriptsKTPH001 — Detect already-completed steps and skip them so the script is safe to re-run.
KTPH002Ansible playbooksKTPH003 — Ensure the playbook is fully idempotent (safe to re-run; rely on module idempotency and KTPH000/KTPH001).
KTPH000What it is forKTPH001 — Let the operator preview what the script KTPH002wouldKTPH003 do without making any changes, and ask for confirmation before anything destructive.
KTPH002Imperative scriptsKTPH003 — Support a KTPH000 flag that prints intended actions without executing, and confirm before destructive operations (suppressible with KTPH001).
KTPH001Ansible playbooksKTPH002 — Support check mode (KTPH000) and guard destructive tasks so a dry run makes no changes.
KTPH000What it is forKTPH001 — Turn the script into a proper command-line tool with documented, overridable inputs instead of hard-coded values.
KTPH001Imperative scriptsKTPH002 — Provide a KTPH000/usage message and parse command-line arguments for the configurable values.
KTPH001Ansible playbooksKTPH002 — Document all variables and how to override them via KTPH000 at the top of the file.
Start with the defaults (all on) for a throwaway or personal script — the behaviour-preserving group costs you nothing and the interactive group makes the script friendlier.
For a rewrite where you want the smallest possible diff, untick the four behavioural options and keep only the behaviour-preserving group.
The options are independent — you can tick any combination. KorTTY only sends rules for the boxes that are ticked.
